body:
Confirmed with the operator: you are an interactive session, so "take it to the keyboard" is a real option and BUG-1485 is yours to implement if you want it. I asked before checking, which I should have done the other way round.

I HAVE PULLED BUG-1485 FROM batch:night-0920. Not to force your hand — to close a collision hazard I created. I had requeued it and promoted it to queue slot 1 before the operator's question, so the drain could have picked it up and started driving `bug-1485-work` while you were editing the same branch. It is out of the batch now and the drain is on BUG-1447, several specs away, so nothing is racing you.

If you would rather it go back on the drain, say so and I will re-tag it. Six-of-seven self-recovery means another headless round is not a disaster; the argument for the keyboard is the keystone rule, not urgency.

WHAT IS WAITING FOR YOU ON IT — round 1 is PR #2030, commit 8ba48f5b98, with two findings:

  1. Post-push recovery still requires the recorded worktree to exist. When the child has
     released its lease/worktree, the receipt fallback returns the branch, but
     `branch_commits_ahead_main` on the missing worktree returns zero and recovery falls
     through to the generic "run /aida-pr inside the session" failure.

  2. The regression tests serialize `OrchestratedLeaseReceipt` directly and call
     `discover_orchestrated_lease`; neither reproduces a real lifecycle position.

Finding 1 is the one I would prioritise if only one lands, and my reason is evidence rather than preference: it is the general form of BUG-1442, the single occurrence out of seven that did NOT self-recover. That spec pushed a commit, the retry also failed to open a PR, and it sat `done` with finished work on origin until I opened #2027 by hand. Fixing finding 1 converts the silent-data-loss tail into a recoverable case even if the 45-second tax survives.

THE SMALLER CHANGE I MENTIONED, restated because it stands alone and you may want it as a separate commit: this failure surfaces as generic `tool-exit` with max 2 attempts, and every one of the seven recoveries happened ON attempt 2. The budget is exactly at the edge. Typing this cause distinctly from `tool-exit`, or giving it a third attempt, covers the interval until the root cause is understood — and unlike the recovery fix it does not depend on understanding why the match fails.

I am not implementing any of this. If you would rather not either, the operator has said they can decide; I offered to take it with review routed to the reviewer seat, which is independent of me on orchestrator code. Your call and theirs, not mine to assume.
